blocks.text: Quantization, introduced from a training focused angle in the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module, is more broadly a general model compression technique applicable at multiple points in a model lifecycle, not just during training, this topic zooms out to cover that fuller picture before the rest of this module dives into specific quantization algorithms.

Understanding quantization as a general concept, not just the QLoRA specific application covered earlier, sets up the remaining topics in this module, INT8, INT4, GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF, each a different specific technique or format within this broader landscape.
1. Quantization as a General Model Compression Technique

blocks.alt: Quantization as a General Model Compression Technique
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248617-218843617.png

At its core, quantization reduces the numeric precision used to represent a model, covered from a training memory perspective in the earlier Quantization Basics topic, but it applies just as much, arguably even more commonly, to already trained models being prepared for efficient deployment.
2. Where Quantization Fits in the Model Lifecycle

blocks.alt: Where Quantization Fits in the Model Lifecycle
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248618-275211082.png

Quantization can be applied during training, as covered with QLoRA in the earlier module, or after training completes, specifically to prepare a finished model for efficient inference, the two use cases share the same underlying numeric ideas but differ meaningfully in their goals and constraints, a distinction the Post-Training Quantization topic later in this module covers directly.
3. Weights vs Activations, What Gets Quantized

blocks.alt: Weights vs Activations, What Gets Quantized
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248618-58720165.png

Most commonly, quantization targets model weights, the values covered throughout this course, but some more aggressive quantization schemes also quantize activations, the intermediate outputs produced during a forward pass, covered in the Gradient Checkpointing topic, for even greater efficiency at some additional complexity.
4. Symmetric vs Asymmetric Quantization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248851-703529476.png

Symmetric quantization maps values around zero using an evenly balanced range, while asymmetric quantization allows the representable range to shift, useful when a set of values is not naturally centered around zero, a design choice that affects how efficiently the limited quantization levels get used.
5. Per-Tensor vs Per-Channel Quantization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248853-77790458.png

Quantization can use a single scaling factor for an entire weight tensor, simple but potentially imprecise, or a separate scaling factor for each channel within that tensor, more precise since it can adapt to how different channels actually vary, at the cost of more overhead to store those additional scaling factors, echoing the double quantization idea covered in the LoRA and QLoRA module.

blocks.text: 6. Calibration, Determining the Right Scale
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248854-41191539.png

Choosing an appropriate quantization scale, how real values map onto the limited representable levels, often relies on calibration, running a small sample of representative data through the model to observe the actual range of values that need to be represented well, a concept explored further in the GPTQ and AWQ topics later in this module.

# A conceptual calibration step
sample_activations = run_forward_pass(model, calibration_dataset)
scale = determine_optimal_scale(sample_activations)

blocks.text: 7. Quantization for Training vs Quantization for Deployment

The QLoRA quantization covered in the earlier module specifically targets making a training run fit in memory, while the techniques covered in the rest of this module, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, more commonly target preparing an already fine-tuned model for efficient deployment and inference, covered further in the Inference and Serving module later in this course.

blocks.title: This framing connects the two quantization discussions across the course
blocks.content: Recognizing that this module quantization topics complement rather than duplicate the training focused QLoRA quantization covered earlier clarifies exactly when each set of techniques applies.

blocks.text: 8. The Quality vs Efficiency Tradeoff, Revisited

Every quantization technique, whether applied during training or after, makes some version of the same fundamental tradeoff introduced in the earlier Quantization Basics topic, reduced numeric precision in exchange for lower memory usage and often faster computation, with different specific techniques finding different points along that tradeoff.
9. A Map of the Quantization Techniques in This Module

blocks.alt: A Map of the Quantization Techniques in This Module
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248854-926632399.png

The remaining topics in this module cover INT8 and INT4 quantization as general numeric formats, then GPTQ and AWQ as specific, more sophisticated quantization algorithms, and GGUF as a popular file format for distributing quantized models, together forming a practical toolkit for the deployment focused side of quantization.
Worked Example

A team that already fine-tuned a model using QLoRA training-time quantization, covered in the earlier module, now wants to deploy that finished model as efficiently as possible for inference, a distinct goal from fitting the original training run in memory.

They apply a post-training quantization technique, covered later in this module, specifically optimized for inference efficiency, recognizing that the QLoRA quantization used during training and the deployment quantization they now need serve related but genuinely different purposes in their model overall lifecycle.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming the QLoRA quantization covered earlier in this course is the same thing as deployment focused quantization
Not understanding the difference between symmetric and asymmetric quantization when configuring a specific technique
Skipping calibration when it would meaningfully improve quantization quality for a given deployment scenario
Treating all quantization techniques as interchangeable rather than recognizing their different tradeoffs and use cases

blocks.text: Practice

In your own words, explain the difference between quantization applied during training, as covered with QLoRA, and quantization applied after training completes for deployment purposes, the focus of the rest of this module.
Key Takeaway

Quantization is a broad model compression technique applicable both during training, as covered through QLoRA in the earlier module, and after training for efficient deployment, the focus of the remaining topics in this module, and understanding concepts like symmetric versus asymmetric ranges, per-tensor versus per-channel granularity, and calibration provides the foundation for the specific techniques, GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF, covered next.
